title: Enemies without hands
hookLine: an enemy with no hands, no feet, no courage and no brains, and still Shantideva calls himself its slave
tomorrow: if a habit has lived in you for ages, can it ever leave?

cards: Here's a strange complaint, deep in chapter four. Shantideva says his enemies have no hands and no feet. They aren't brave.
They aren't clever. And somehow he's their slave. That sounds like a riddle until it's one in the morning and a glowing screen is still in your hand.
The phone can't grab anyone by the collar. Nobody is forcing the thumb to keep moving. Still, another hour is gone.
So how does something with no hands win every single fight?

teach.b: First, who these enemies are. Shantideva names them: craving, anger, and the rest of the kleshas, the afflictions that stir up the mind. Not people.
Not demons outside the door. Moods and pulls that rise inside. Now the riddle.
They have no hands of their own, so they borrow yours. Craving doesn't lift the phone; you do, while craving whispers. Anger doesn't type the text; your fingers do, while anger dictates.
That's the answer to the puzzle: an enemy without hands wins by living inside the one who has them. Shantideva makes it sharper.
These enemies sit right in his own mind, he says, and strike him from there at their ease, and he puts up with it, calm as anything.
He calls that patience in the wrong place. He'd never let an outside attacker move in and set up house. Here's the hopeful part, and it's the reason the verse exists.
If the enemy works through your hands, your hands are also where the fight happens.
The first move isn't a battle. It's spotting.
Seeing the pull for what it is, a visitor with no hands, before your own hands do its work.

how: Buddhist teachers often begin work with the afflictions (kleshas) by simple recognition: noticing craving or anger as it arises and naming it, before trying to change it.

o: rivals who work against you quietly behind your back
inner pulls like craving that move you with your own hands
bad luck that arrives when nobody is to blame for it

games.q: the riddle, solved — tap the pairs.
p: spotting the pull for what it is

s: Shantideva's enemies here are the people who wronged him
they're afflictions, like craving and anger, living in his own mind.
the poem says these enemies aren't brave or clever
no hands, no feet, no courage, no wisdom, and still they rule him.
Shantideva praises putting up with these enemies calmly
he calls that patience in the wrong place.

games.q: you've meant to call your grandmother all week. every evening you end up scrolling instead. in Shantideva's terms, what's beating you?
o: the phone itself: it's built to grab you, so it's out of your hands.
a craving inside, using your own hands to keep you scrolling.
your schedule: there truly hasn't been a free minute all week.
games.why: the enemy has no hands; it borrows yours. seeing the craving is the first move, and the call is still in reach.

practice: Think back over the last day to one moment when something pulled you off course: a scroll, a snap, a second helping you didn't want. Say its name out loud, quietly, in two words, like craving, again.
Then rest your hands open on your knees and stay with how ordinary they look.

wordCard.voice: Enemies without hands: Shantideva's name for craving and anger. They can't move a finger, so they use ours.

orig.note: Sanskrit: affliction, a disturbing emotion; Pali kilesa. Craving and anger are the usual examples.

carryVoice: Carry this: no hands, no feet, and still it moves you, until you see it. Two days into chapter four.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 4.28-4.29 (enemies such as craving and hatred have no hands or feet, are neither brave nor wise, yet enslave me; dwelling in my mind they strike me at will, and I bear it, a misplaced patience)
